strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and well-motivated problem in TAMP: reducing the manual effort of constructing PDDL domains and interfacing them with motion planners.

The proposed framework (PDDLLM with predicate imagination via simulation roll-outs and action invention in logical space) is technically coherent, and the LoCA component that automatically maps logical action effects into motion-planning constraints is a nice, practical contribution that removes a known manual bottleneck.

The evaluation is extensive by robotics/LLM-planning standards: over 1,200 tasks across 9 environments, 6 baselines plus an ablation (RuleAsMem), comparison against reasoning LLMs (o1, R1) with extended time limits, token-cost analysis, planning-time-limit variations, prompt-robustness tests, and degraded-demonstration experiments.

Demonstrated deployment on three physical robot platforms (Agilex Piper, Franka Panda, UR5e) and integration with a fine-tuned VLA policy as an alternative execution layer, which supports the claim of practical applicability and flexibility across classical and learned control.

The domain-quality analysis (missing/redundant predicates and actions vs. expert-designed domains, Table 3) and the suboptimal-demonstration study (Table 4) provide useful insight beyond raw success rates, and the paper is generally honest about limitations (e.g., missing predicates in bridge building, reliance on expert refinement).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior work. Predicate invention and domain learning from demonstrations is well explored (Silver et al. 2023; Han et al. InterPreT 2024; Huang et al. 2025; Curtis et al. 2022), and the 'first method' claim in the introduction and conclusion is overstated. The core novelty is essentially a prompting pipeline (summarize simulation roll-outs into predicates, summarize logical state transitions into actions) plus LoCA; the latter is conceptually simple (retrieve inequality constraints attached to predicates and apply them sequentially in the motion planner).

The method relies on substantial privileged information that undercuts the 'from a single demonstration' framing: the feature space assumes access to ground-truth object poses, colors, and sizes; real-world data collection uses ArUco markers and CAD models (Section A.12); and demonstrations must be segmented into logical state transitions. The system is far from deriving domains from raw sensory input, and the perception gap is only briefly acknowledged in the conclusion.

The experimental tasks are largely tabletop block-manipulation-style domains with pre-known feature types (position, color, size). It remains unclear how the approach scales to genuinely diverse object geometry, articulated or deformable objects, or open-ended feature spaces where the fixed set of feature dimensions and partitions may not apply. The complexity analysis in A.10 is informal.

Several baselines are reimplementations or adaptations rather than direct comparisons to published systems for domain learning (e.g., the closest domain-inference competitors like Han et al. 2024 or Huang et al. 2025 are discussed in related work but not empirically compared), so the claim of superiority over 'six LLM-based planning baselines' is partly against variants of the authors' own construction (LLMTAMP, -FF, -FR) that receive weaker inputs than PDDLLM's compiled domains.

Some methodological details are under-specified: how the demonstration is segmented into logical actions when predicates are noisy, how the hyperparameter u (feature subspace size) and the number of partitions are chosen per task, and how the parallel-prompting candidate selection/pruning works. This affects reproducibility, and no code release is mentioned.

The apparent fairness of some comparisons is questionable: PDDLLM performs expensive offline domain derivation (parallel LLM prompting, simulation roll-outs) whose cost is not fully accounted in the token-cost comparison, while baselines are charged per-instance inference; the success-rate gap over RuleAsMem (the ablation using the same generated domain without a symbolic solver) also suggests much of the gain comes from the symbolic planner rather than from domain derivation quality per se.

strengths: Extensive evaluation: over 1,200 tasks across nine simulated environments, three time-limit settings, and comparisons against six LLM-based planning variants including reasoning-model backbones (o1, DeepSeek-R1), which is above the norm for this area.
The system addresses a genuinely important problem in TAMP: reducing the manual burden of designing PDDL domains and interfacing symbolic plans with motion planners (LoCA).
Real-robot deployment on three platforms (Agilex Piper, Franka Panda, UR5e), including a VLA-integration experiment, provides evidence beyond simulation.
The paper includes useful analyses on suboptimal demonstrations, missing/redundant domain elements, token costs, and prompt-variation robustness (Appendix A.7).
Writing and figures are generally clear, and the prompt templates in the appendix support reproducibility of the methodology.
weaknesses: The central 'no manual predesign' claim is overstated. The method presupposes a manually defined feature space (position, orientation, size, color), manually specified scene-description templates, interval partitions with a user-set hyperparameter u, and demonstrations augmented with object CAD models and ArUco markers (A.12). Much of the human effort appears shifted from predicate design to these hidden components, rather than eliminated.

Novelty over prior work is incremental. Predicate invention from data (Silver et al. 2023; Curtis et al. 2022; VisualPredicator; InterPreT) and automated domain inference with LLMs (Huang et al. 2025; Oswald et al. 2025; Guan et al. 2023) are closely related, yet none of these closest competitors are empirically compared against; the baselines are mostly self-reimplemented variants of generic LLM planners (LLMTAMP/FF/FR).

The demonstration requirements undercut the 'single demonstration' framing: for compositional tasks (rearrangement, bridge building) multiple demonstrations from simpler tasks are needed, and the demonstration collection pipeline itself is labor-intensive.

Missing predicate rates are high for the harder domains (e.g., 22% for bridge building), and the authors attribute failure precisely to this; the mechanism to ensure coverage of necessary predicates (subspace sampling) is not shown to scale or be complete, and there is no analysis of when/why sampling misses critical predicates.

Ablations are thin: the only true ablation is RuleAsMem. There is no ablation isolating the contribution of physical simulation rollouts versus LLM prior knowledge alone, no sensitivity analysis on the partition hyperparameters in the main results, and the parallel-prompting refinement (>5 prompts) reads as a heuristic patch rather than a principled mechanism.

Some evidence is ambiguous: Table 2 shows PDDLLM incurs substantially higher token cost than the strongest weak baseline (LLMTAMP: 99k vs 415k overall), and the 50s/100s success-rate gaps in Appendix Tables 7-8 for rearrangement are modest; statistical rigor rests on only three runs.
The Expert Design baseline is initialized from PDDLLM-derived domains and then refined, which weakens it as a true upper-bound comparison and may bias the domain-quality analysis.
Reproducibility is limited: dependence on the closed GPT-4o API, an in-house demonstration-capture rig, and no stated code release.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: reducing the manual engineering burden of constructing PDDL domains for TAMP, which is a recognized bottleneck in long-horizon robotic planning.

The proposed framework (PDDLLM) is technically sensible: combining LLM reasoning with physically verified simulation roll-outs to ground predicates, deriving actions from logical state transitions in the demonstration, and the LoCA module that automatically maps first-order predicate constraints into motion-planning constraints is a genuine contribution toward fully automated symbol-to-motion grounding.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: over 1,200 tasks across nine environments, six baselines plus an ablation, comparisons against reasoning LLMs (o1, R1) with extended time limits, token-cost and time-cost analyses, time-limit sensitivity (25s/50s/100s), prompt-variation robustness tests, suboptimal-demonstration experiments, and domain-quality analysis (missing/redundant predicates vs. expert domains).
Real-robot deployment on three platforms (Agilex Piper, Franka Panda, UR5e), including integration with a finetuned π0 VLA policy, supports the practicality claims beyond simulation.

The token-efficiency argument is well made: once the domain is derived offline, planning requires little LLM inference at test time, which is a meaningful practical advantage over reasoning-LLM baselines and is substantiated by Table 5 timing data.
Knowledge transfer experiments (composing actions from multiple simple demonstrations) and the suboptimal/noisy demonstration study (Table 4) probe robustness in ways many similar papers do not.
weaknesses: Strong reliance on privileged, ground-truth information that limits the real autonomy claim: the method assumes a perfect perception function providing continuous object states, and in the real-world setup object properties come from CAD models and poses from ArUco markers. The 'fully automated' framing understates these assumptions; integrating perception is deferred to future work.

The 'Expert Design' baseline is initialized from PDDLLM-generated outputs and then refined by an expert. This circular construction weakens the upper-bound comparison and raises the possibility that expert domains inherit PDDLLM's structure, biasing the domain-quality analysis (Table 3) and Q3 conclusions.

Novelty relative to prior work is not fully delineated. Predicate invention (Silver et al. 2023), LLM-guided domain extension (Liang et al. 2024; Athalye et al. 2024; Byrnes et al. 2024), and LLM-based domain generation from descriptions (Oswald et al. 2025; Guan et al. 2023) exist; the claim of being 'the first method to construct planning domains without manual predesign' is strong, and the delta over the closest prior systems could be more carefully justified.

Key hyperparameters and design choices are under-analyzed: the feature subspace partition size u is described as configurable but its sensitivity, selection procedure, and failure modes when boundaries are misspecified are not systematically studied. Similarly, reliance on a 'predefined scene-description template' for prompts is acknowledged but its generality is unclear.

The evaluation uses mostly custom reimplementations of baselines (LLMTAMP, LLMTAMP-FF/FR) rather than released code from the original papers, and there is no mention of code release, which limits reproducibility.

All main results use GPT-4o as the single LLM backbone; while reasoning-LLM baselines are included, there is no ablation of PDDLLM itself across different LLM backbones, leaving open how much of the success is attributable to the framework versus the specific model's priors (e.g., the LLM must still name predicates like is_on and produce valid PDDL syntax).

Failure cases are acknowledged (missing complex predicates in bridge building/burger cooking) but the analysis of why the LLM fails on such predicates and how to detect/repair them is thin; success rates drop noticeably there (64-87%).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: automating planning-domain construction for TAMP reduces a major engineering bottleneck, and the paper targets the full pipeline (predicates, actions, and automatic interfacing with motion planners via LoCA), which is more end-to-end than most prior domain-inference work.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 1,200 tasks across nine environments, multiple baselines including reasoning LLMs (o1, R1), ablations over parallel prompting count, discretization hyperparameter, LLM backbones (Qwen3), and time limits, plus prompt-variation robustness tests.

Real-world validation on three physical robot platforms (Agilex Piper, Franka Panda, UR5e) and a demonstration of compatibility with a learned VLA (Pi0) policy as the low-level executor, which strengthens practical significance.
Good token/cost analysis showing that reasoning happens once offline at domain-derivation time rather than per-task, an practically important property for long-term robot deployment.
Honest limitation section and thorough appendix (predicate examples, prompt templates, noise-resistance experiments), which aids reproducibility and credibility.
weaknesses: The claim of 'no manual predesign / fully automated' is overstated: the method still requires a hand-defined continuous feature space (position, orientation, size, color), a discretization scheme, predefined scene-description templates for prompting, and a predicate-to-inequality grounding convention in LoCA. The level of implicit human prior knowledge should be characterized more carefully.

Missing head-to-head comparisons with the most closely related domain-inference methods (e.g., Silver et al. 2023 predicate invention, Guan et al. 2023 world-model construction, Han et al. 2024 INTERPRET, Liang et al. 2024 VisualPredicator, Huang et al. 2025). The strongest baselines are LLM-planner variants without domain learning, which weakens the central claim of superiority over state-of-the-art domain inference.
The domain-quality assessment (Table 3) is partly circular: expert-designed domains are 'refined from PDDLLM-derived domains by an expert,' which could bias the missing/redundant analysis.

LoCA's automatic motion-constraint generation only handles first-order predicates in the action effect set; higher-order predicates and complex dynamics (deformables, tight-tolerance tasks) fall outside its scope, limiting generality of the claimed automatic grounding.

Some technical/presentation issues undermine polish: Table 6 lists 'o1-TAMP' twice (apparently meant to include R1-TAMP), inconsistent spellings ('Hannoi'), and the 'first approach to generate a complete planning domain from scratch' claim needs more careful qualification given the existing predicate/domain-invention literature.

Simulation evaluation is confined to rigid tabletop manipulation with ArUco/CAD-based state; only three runs per condition for success rates; sim-to-real gap in domain derivation (domains learned in simulation, deployed on real robots) is not quantified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely relevant problem (automating planning-domain construction for TAMP) and positions itself reasonably clearly against prior domain-inference work.

The evaluation scale is large: 1,200 tasks across nine environments, multiple time-limit settings, ablations on hyperparameters (u, number of parallel prompts), LLM backbone swaps (Qwen3-4B/8B), and deployment on three physical robot platforms plus a VLA (π0) integration.

The idea of using physical simulation roll-outs to ground discretized feature subspaces into predicates with explicit inequality constraints, and to interface them automatically with a motion planner (LoCA), is a coherent and interpretable system design.

Ablations such as domain-quality comparison against expert-designed domains (missing/redundant predicate rates) and perception-noise robustness experiments provide some insight beyond raw success rates.
weaknesses: Missing the most important baselines: the paper claims to outperform LLM-based planning methods, yet the direct competitors for domain inference from demonstrations (Guan et al. 2023, Han et al. 2024, Liang et al. 2024, Huang et al. 2025, Oswald et al. 2024, Silver et al. 2023) are cited and discussed but never actually compared against. The six baselines are all self-implemented variants of the same LLMTAMP prompting idea 'inspired by' prior work, making the central superiority claim weakly supported.

The 'Expert Design' baseline is circular: expert-crafted domains are 'initialized with PDDLLM-generated outputs' and then refined. This is an unusual construction that blurs the comparison against true human-designed domains.

The claim of 'minimal manual domain initialization' and 'no predefined predicates or actions' is overstated. The method requires a hand-designed feature space (position, orientation, size, color), known object properties from CAD/URDF, ArUco-marker perception, axis-aligned interval discretization with hand-initialized u_f, and motion feasibility that reduces to simple interval inequalities — assumptions that effectively predetermine what predicates can be discovered and restrict the method to structured tabletop manipulation.

Methodological artifacts undermine polish and credibility: Section B.13 contains the sentence 'To address your concern,' which is clearly leftover rebuttal text; Table 6 lists 'o1-TAMP o1-TAMP' (presumably R1-TAMP) as duplicate column headers; repeated typos ('Tower of Hannoi', 'suas', 'We the selection of u_f'). These suggest the manuscript was not carefully assembled.

Cost accounting is one-sided: PDDLLM requires thousands of parallel physical simulations per domain derivation plus ~300-500k tokens for domain generation, yet simulation compute and generation-time cost are excluded from the efficiency comparisons; token-cost comparisons favor PDDLLM only because execution-time reasoning is offloaded to a PDDL solver, whereas baselines are penalized for test-time prompting.

Fairness of baseline setup is questionable: baselines are given the demonstration as natural language and a list of actions 'to choose from', i.e., a partially predefined action space, while PDDLLM uses the same demonstrations to build the domain — the comparison measures prompt formulation as much as domain inference.

The headline claim of being 'the first approach to generate a complete planning domain from scratch, without relying on any predefined predicates or actions' is an overclaim given the engineered feature space and constraint templates described above.

Evidence for domain quality is mixed and downplayed: Table 3 shows 22.2% missing predicates on the hardest tasks, and the paper's own limitation section admits the system misses ordering predicates like (all_base_finished), degrading planning under time budgets; success rates are near-saturated on easy tasks, so aggregate numbers overstate the differences.
No code release or artifact is mentioned; the reproducibility statement only points to appendix sections of the paper itself, which limits reproducibility of a heavily engineering-dependent pipeline.
Statistical rigor is thin: only three parallel runs per condition, and error bars on near-100% success rates on simple tasks add little information.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: automating planning-domain construction for TAMP, which addresses a genuine bottleneck in applying symbolic long-horizon planning to robotics.

The pipeline is well designed and end-to-end: predicate imagination grounded in physics simulation, action invention from logical state transitions, and automatic interfacing with motion planners (LoCA) remove the need for predefined primitives or manual domain-engineering, which differentiates it from most prior domain-inference work.

Extensive evaluation: 1,200+ tasks across nine environments, comparisons against multiple LLM-based baselines including reasoning models (o1, R1), an expert-designed upper bound, and an ablation (RuleAsMem) that isolates the value of the symbolic solver.

Thorough supplementary analysis: ablations on the discretization hyperparameter u, number of parallel prompts, LLM backbones (Qwen vs. GPT-4o), planning time limits, prompt-style robustness, perception noise tolerance, and token/time cost — this level of ablation is above average for submissions in this area.

Real-robot deployment on three platforms (Franka, Agilex Piper, UR5e) plus integration with a VLA policy demonstrates practical applicability beyond simulation, and the domain-correction experiments (Table 4) probe an interesting property of the method.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are limited and largely self-implemented. The paper does not compare against established domain/predicate-inference methods it cites as closely related (e.g., Silver et al. 2023, Guan et al. 2023, Liang et al. 2024, Huang et al. 2025). The main baselines are variants of a common LLM-TAMP template constructed by the authors, which weakens the claim of superiority over the state of the art in domain learning specifically.

Claims of 'minimal manual initialization' should be scrutinized: the feature space definition, feature discretization scheme, scene-description templates, physical constraint formats, and the coupling to a structured simulator/CAD models all embed substantial task-family-specific engineering. The system essentially automates domain writing within a fairly rigid predefined scaffolding, and its scope is explicitly limited to rigid-object tabletop TAMP domains (Section B.14), which is narrower than the framing suggests.

The 'first approach to generate a complete planning domain from scratch' claim in the conclusion is overreaching given cited prior work on LLM-based domain generation (Oswald et al. 2024, Guan et al. 2023, Han et al. 2024); positioning and novelty claims need softening.

The expert-design baseline is initialized from PDDLLM-generated outputs and refined by an expert, which conflates expert effort with PDDLLM scaffolding and makes the 'closely matches expert performance' comparison less informative than presented.

Some statistical rigor is thin: three parallel runs for headline success rates, small real-robot samples (10 trials/task), and success-rate definitions that depend on a fixed 50-second budget whose justification is somewhat arbitrary. Also, missing-predicate rates up to ~22% for complex tasks (Table 3) partly undercut the 'high-quality domains' narrative and are only partially analyzed.

Reproducibility is limited in practice: the method depends on proprietary GPT-4o behavior and thousands of simulation roll-outs; no code release is mentioned, and much of the pipeline detail lives in an appendix with heavy prompt engineering, making exact reproduction difficult for others.
